newsitem.title: UK: Alarms ring as dlr/mark's 1.4-1.8 band in danger.
newsitem.headline: Alarms ring as dlr/mark's 1.4-1.8 band in danger.

text.p: A recent history of central bank intervention on exchange rates shows the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) has not been happy with the dollar/mark much above 1.80 or below 1.40 this decade.
The dollar's recent surge to the top of this range is expected to rekindle speculation about whether the G7 will agree on a coordinated protest against the move, said analysts.

The tone of comments from German finance minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday reinforced these concerns after he said currency markets were overreacting and Germany had been in regular contact with its G7 partners on the issue.

"It's clear we are already in discomfort zones for central bankers, who have been trying verbally to stabilise the situation (for dollar/mark) since the 1.60s," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in Europe.

"The bigger question is what they could do to back up any intervention," he said. "Until the market feels a German interest rate rise is a more credible threat, then the prospect of such intervention will only act as a temporary drag."

Just one month after the successful G7 intervention to cap the dollar above 1.80 in July 1991, the Bundesbank raised both its discount and Lombard interest rates. A month later the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its discount rate.

Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro, said the recent fall in German interest rate futures may suggest the market has become more nervous about the Bundesbank's reaction to mark weakness. There has been talk it may nudge rates higher if the mark continues in freefall, he said.
The implied yield on the three-month September Euromark futures contract has risen 10 basis points this week to 3.25 percent. The central bank's key two-week repurchase rate is 3.0 percent.
"We know the Bundesbank is unhappy with the mark weakening much further from here but it's interesting to see Waigel as the first politician on board," said Geddes.
"The basic intervention principles still apply, however, and they will need more of an element of surprise and some better backing from the fundamentals for a coordinated move to work."

The currency options market, closely watched by central banks for sentiment, shows a distinct bias for mark puts against the dollar and pound. But pricing is not as extreme as it is for dollar/yen puts, for example, and this suggests the market is not overstretched.

"If they (G7) allow dollar/mark above 1.80, they are admitting there has been a sea-change in fundamentals to justify the dollar rising to levels not seen before in the 1990s," said a senior trader at a French bank in London.
Senior finance officials and central bankers are typically keen to play down recurrent speculation that agreed "comfort zones" for the major global exchange rates even exist.
But their own actions suggest the 40 pfennig round-figure trading range between 1.40 and 1.80 is where they would prefer the dollar to remain, analysts said.

The last time there was concerted central bank action to sell dollars for marks was in the summer of 1991, when the Federal Reserve, the Bundesbank and several European central banks intervened as the dollar broke above 1.80.
The dollar had risen steeply against the mark from then- record lows in February about 1.44 as consumer confidence in the U.S. soared in the wake of the Gulf War.

Intervention by the European banks to smooth the dollar's steep rise was intermittent from as early as late spring of that year and as low as about 1.60. But the Fed only joined the intervention above 1.80 after a G7 meeting in late June 1991.

The dollar topped out at 1.8430 that month and, barring a one-day spectacular surge during on the Soviet coup attempt in August, it continued falling to new record lows in September 1992, again prompting concerted action from G7 central banks to support it.

The subsequent dollar peak at 1.7686 in February 1994 did not need overt G7 coordination to turn the dollar around but there was constant speculation at the time that the Bundesbank was selling part of huge dollar reserves accumulated during the European currency crisis of 1992.
A relatively quiet period of trading for dollar/mark ensued but a fresh surge of the mark to below 1.40 in early 1995 saw a return of the G7 central banks to again shore up dollar losses.
